source_text: Diximus, quantum mediocritati nostrae licuit, de universis quae Baptismi religionem struunt; nunc ad reliquum statum ejus, aeque ut potero, progrediar de quaestiunculis quibusdam. Baptismus ab Joanne denuntiatus jam tunc habuit quaestionem ab ipso quidem Domino propositam Pharisaeis, coelestisne is Baptismus esset, an vero terrenus? De quo illi non valuerunt constanter respondere, utpote non intelligentes, quia non credentes. Nos porro quantula fide sumus, tantulo et intellectu possumus aestimare, divinum quidem eum Baptismum fuisse, mandatu tamen, non et potestate, quod et Joannem a Domino missum legimus in hoc munus caeterum humanum conditione. Nihil enim coeleste praestabat, sed coelestibus praeministrabat, poenitentiae scilicet praepositus, quae est in hominis potestate. Denique legis doctores et Pharisaei, qui credere noluerunt, nec poenitentiam egere. Quod si poenitentia humanum est, et Baptismus ipsius ejusdem conditionis fuerit necesse est; aut daret et Spiritum Sanctum et remissionem delictorum, si coelestis fuisset. Sed neque peccatum dimittit, neque Spiritum indulget, nisi Deus solus. Etiam ipse Dominus, nisi ipse prius ascenderet ad Patrem, aliter negavit, Spiritum descensurum. Id quod Dominus nondum conferebat, servus utique praestare non posset. Adeo postea in Actis apostolorum invenimus, quoniam qui Joannis Baptismum habebant, non accepissent Spiritum sanctum, quem ne auditu quidem noverant: ergo non erat coeleste, quod coelestia non exhibebat: cum ipsum quod coeleste in Joanne fuerat, spiritus prophetiae, post totius spiritus in Dominum translationem usque adeo defecerit, ut quem praedicaverat, quem advenientem designaverat, postmodum, an ipse esset miserit sciscitatum. Agebatur itaque Baptismus poenitentiae, quasi canditatus remissionis et sanctificationis in Christo subsecuturae. Nam quod praedicabat Baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem delictorum, in futuram remissionem enuntiatum est. Siquidem poenitentia antecedit, remissio subsequitur, et hoc est viam praeparare: qui autem praeparat, non idem ipse perficit, sed alii perficiendum procurat. Ipse profitetur sua non esse coelestia, sed Christi, dicendo: Qui de terra est, de terra loquitur: qui de supernis venit, super omnes est. Item, in sola poenitentia tinguere; venturum mox, qui tingueret in spiritu et igni. Scilicet, quia vera et stabilis aquae fides qua tinguitur in salutem; simulata autem et infirma, igni tinguitur in judicium.
pass_a_gloss: We have spoken, as much as our mediocrity has allowed, about all things which pertain to the religion of Baptism; now I will proceed, as much as I am able, to the remaining state of it, concerning certain little questions. Baptism, which was announced by John, already had a question proposed by the Lord himself to the Pharisees, whether that Baptism was heavenly or truly earthly? About which those people were not able to respond constantly, as they were not understanding, because they were not believing. We, furthermore, with as much faith as we are, are also able to estimate with as much understanding, that that Baptism was indeed divine, but by command, not also by power, which we also read that John was sent by the Lord into this duty, nonetheless human in condition. For he was not exhibiting anything heavenly, but was serving heavenly things, namely, having been put in charge of repentance, which is in human power. Finally, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, who were unwilling to believe, also did not undergo repentance. Which, if repentance is human, it is necessary that the Baptism of it was also of the same condition; or it would have given both the Holy Spirit and the remission of sins, if it had been heavenly. But neither does it forgive sin, nor does it grant the Spirit, except God alone. Also, the Lord himself, unless he had first ascended to the Father, otherwise denied that the Spirit would descend. What the Lord was not yet conferring, a servant was certainly not able to provide. So much so that afterwards we find in the Acts of the Apostles, that those who had the Baptism of John had not received the Holy Spirit, whom they had not even known by hearing: therefore, it was not heavenly, because it was not exhibiting heavenly things: since the very thing that was heavenly in John, the spirit of prophecy, failed after the translation of the whole Spirit into the Lord, so much so that what he had predicted, what he had designated as coming, afterwards, he inquired whether he himself had sent. Therefore, the Baptism was being administered for repentance, as a candidate for the remission and sanctification in Christ that would follow. For what he was preaching, a Baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, was announced for a future remission. Indeed, repentance precedes, remission follows, and this is to prepare the way: he who prepares, does not himself perfect, but procures for others to perfect. He himself professes that his things are not heavenly, but Christ's, saying: He who is from the earth, speaks from the earth: he who comes from what is above, is above all. Also, to baptize only in repentance; soon to come, he who would baptize in Spirit and fire. Clearly, because the true and stable faith of water, by which one is baptized for salvation; but the simulated and weak, is baptized in fire for judgment.

pass_b_english: I have said what my limited gifts allowed about everything that constitutes the religion of Baptism; now I will move on, as best I can, to its remaining aspect — certain minor questions. The Baptism announced by John already raised a question posed by the Lord himself to the Pharisees: was that Baptism heavenly or earthly? They could not give a steady answer, since they did not understand, because they did not believe. We, for our part, can gauge it only to the measure of our faith and understanding: that Baptism was indeed divine, but by command, not by power. We read that John was sent by the Lord to perform this duty, yet his condition was human. He displayed nothing heavenly; he served heavenly things, having been put in charge of repentance — and repentance lies within human power. Finally, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, who refused to believe, also refused to repent. If repentance is human, then the Baptism tied to it must share that same condition; otherwise it would have bestowed both the Holy Spirit and the remission of sins, had it been heavenly. But it neither forgives sin nor grants the Spirit — only God does that. Even the Lord himself denied that the Spirit would descend unless he first ascended to the Father (John 3:31). What the Lord had not yet conferred, a servant certainly could not supply. This is confirmed in Acts: those who had received John's Baptism had not received the Holy Spirit — they had not even heard of him (Acts 19:1-6). Therefore, it was not heavenly, because it did not exhibit heavenly gifts. Even the heavenly element in John — the spirit of prophecy — failed after the full transfer of the Spirit to the Lord, to the point that John, who had predicted and identified the Coming One, later sent to ask whether he himself was the one who had been sent. Thus John's Baptism was administered for repentance, as a candidate awaiting the remission and sanctification in Christ that would follow. His preaching of a Baptism of repentance for the remission of sins pointed to a future remission. Repentance precedes; remission follows. That is what it means to prepare the way: the one who prepares does not himself perfect, but arranges for another to perfect. John himself confesses that what belongs to him is not heavenly, but Christ's, saying: "He who is from the earth speaks from the earth; he who comes from above is above all." He baptized only in repentance; the One coming soon would baptize in Spirit and fire. Clearly, true and stable faith in the water baptizes for salvation; simulated and weak faith is baptized in fire for judgment.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the distinction between 'mandatu' (command) and 'potestate' (power), and the relationship between repentance and remission. Pass A is a faithful literal gloss, and Pass B is a fluent translation that correctly incorporates the required scripture citations (John 3:31 and Acts 19:1-6) to identify the alluded passages. All clauses are accounted for.
